The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is a statutory body constituted under Section 45ZB of the RBI Act to fix the benchmark policy interest rate.
The MPC comprises six members: the RBI Governor as chairperson, four external members appointed by the government, and one RBI official nominated by the central bank.
The primary mandate of the MPC is to maintain price stability while keeping in mind the objective of growth, targeting consumer inflation.
Liquidity management involves various instruments like the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF), repo rate, reverse repo rate, and Open Market Operations (OMOs).

explain.headline: UPSC Editorial Analysis: Public Interest Litigation
static: Article 32 of the Constitution provides the right to move the Supreme Court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights, guaranteed as a fundamental right itself.
Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs including habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo-warranto, and certiorari for enforcement of fundamental rights and other purposes.
Public Interest Litigation (PIL) was pioneered in the late 1970s and early 1980s by judges like Justice P.N. Bhagwati and Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer, relaxing the strict locus standi rule.
Suo motu cognizance allows courts to take up matters on their own motion without a formal petition being filed by an affected party, based on media reports or letters.
The separation of powers under the Indian Constitution ensures checks and balances between the legislature, executive, and judiciary, though judicial activism occasionally blurs these lines.

explain.background: Post-Emergency judicial activism relaxed locus standi to grant marginalized citizens access to justice through PILs and suo motu actions, though concerns over judicial overreach have grown.
significance: It addresses the dual challenge of ensuring access to justice for the voiceless while preventing judicial overreach and backlog.
It evaluates comparative global practices in public law litigation from South Africa, the US, UK, and Germany.
It provides actionable structural reforms for Indian courts to balance judicial activism with institutional separation of powers.

points: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar termed Article 32 the heart and soul of the Constitution, forming with Article 226 the primary shield against state overreach.
Post-Emergency, the Supreme Court relaxed locus standi rules, creating Public Interest Litigation and suo motu cognizance to empower marginalized citizens.
Originally meant for bonded laborers and undertrials, these powers face criticism today for becoming selective, media-driven, and overburdened by policy matters.
Suo motu actions often lack codified objective criteria, tending to track high-visibility media cycles or urban elite concerns instead of silent human rights issues.
The PIL mechanism frequently shifts from public interest to publicity or political interest, used to settle commercial rivalries or delay infrastructure projects.
The Supreme Court's advice to exhaust Article 226 remedies first can cause prolonged detentions in urgent personal liberty cases involving habeas corpus and bail.
Judicial initiatives have successfully corrected executive inertia during disaster responses, pandemic management, and custodial torture.
Global models like South Africa, the US, the UK, and Germany use screening rules, leave requirements, and political question doctrines to regulate public interest litigation.
Proposed reforms include forming permanent screening committees, imposing exemplary costs on frivolous petitions, and establishing dedicated benches for personal liberty.
sum.text:
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar termed Article 32 the “heart and soul” of the Constitution because a right without a judicial remedy is a hollow promise. Alongside Article 226 (High Courts), it forms the primary shield protecting citizens against state overreach.
Post-Emergency, the Supreme Court relaxed the rigid doctrine of locus standi . This birthed Public Interest Litigation (PIL) and suo motu cognizance .
Originally intended to empower marginalized citizens (e.g., bonded laborers, undertrials), these extraordinary powers face criticism today for becoming selective, media-driven, and overburdened by policy matters.
Selective Suo Motu Cognizance: Unlike regular civil and criminal appeals, suo motu actions often lack codified, objective criteria. Critics argue that interventions tend to track high-visibility media cycles or urban elite concerns (e.g., city pollution, high-profile institutional conflicts), while systemic, silent human rights issues struggle for equal urgency.

Parties often use PILs to settle commercial rivalries, delay infrastructure projects, or resolve political disputes, occupying excessive judicial bench time.

static: The Election Commission of India is an autonomous constitutional authority responsible for administering election processes in India under Article 324 of the Constitution.

The Baranwal case (Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India) judgment by the Supreme Court mandated an independent panel consisting of the Prime Minister, Leader of Opposition, and Chief Justice of India for ECI appointments.
Parliament subsequently enacted a law in 2023 replacing the Chief Justice of India with a Union Cabinet Minister in the selection committee for Election Commissioners.
Split verdicts in the Supreme Court occur when a bench of two judges disagrees, requiring the matter to be referred to a larger bench for final adjudication.

explain.headline: Smart Cities Mission Critique: Why Political Dreaming Cannot Replace Urban Planning
static: The Smart Cities Mission was launched in June 2015 by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) to promote cities that provide core infrastructure and give a decent quality of life to citizens.
Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) derive their primary constitutional mandate and backing from the 74th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992, which added Part IX-A to the Constitution of India.
Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) under the SCM were incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, functioning as limited companies to plan, approve, implement, and manage smart city projects.

The 74th Constitutional Amendment envisaged urban local bodies as institutions of self-government, though fiscal devolution and administrative capacity remain persistent structural challenges across Indian states.
explain.what: An opinion piece arguing that the Smart Cities Mission suffered from structural flaws inherent to political 'dream projects', prioritizing visible enclaves, top-down governance, and public relations over foundational urban needs.
explain.why_in_news: The article critically evaluates the record of the Smart Cities Mission now that the Mission has formally ended.
explain.background: Urban development in India is constitutionally mandated to be managed by elected Urban Local Bodies, but central missions have frequently bypassed local governance through parallel implementation bodies.
significance: Highlights the structural weaknesses of India's third tier of urban local governance.
Critiques the preference for photogenic, capital-intensive projects over foundational civic needs like drainage, public transport, and housing.
Provides valuable perspective for civil services aspirants on democratic decentralization and urban planning failures.
prelims: A 2025 study by Sarbeswar Praharaj found that SCM interventions reached less than 10 per cent of the population across 100 cities.
A 2021 study by Bajpai and Biberman showed nearly 40 per cent of Smart Cities transport funding went to roads and parking.
Odisha's Jaga Mission is cited as a successful ground-up urban initiative that prioritized social context and daily use.
explain.mains: Examine the structural limitations of top-down urban development models in India, with special reference to the Smart Cities Mission. How can decentralized urban governance be strengthened to address local civic needs? (15 Marks)
explain.video_query: Smart Cities Mission India analysis urban planning critique

stories.ai_why: Critique of the Smart Cities Mission provides valuable insights for urban governance.

points: The Smart Cities Mission (SCM) was India's largest political dream project in urban history, and its conclusion invites critical scrutiny of urban planning.
Dream projects rely on state narratives of radical transformation and public relations rather than expert input, citizen experience, or rigorous feasibility.
The SCM used an Area-Based Development (ABD) model that concentrated massive investments in tiny enclaves, reaching less than 10 per cent of the population in many cities.
Projects bypassed municipal bodies by operating through parallel Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs), further weakening India's constitutionally fragile third tier of local governance.
Instead of addressing contextual local needs like drainage or affordable housing, SCM favored visible capital works such as roads, parking, and digital command centres.
A 2021 study by Bajpai and Biberman noted that nearly 40 per cent of SCM transport funds went to roads and parking, compared to only 2 per cent for buses.
The Mission's visual politics used aerial and drone imagery to showcase mastery over landscape while turning citizens into mere passive props or audiences.
Unlike top-down political dreams, ground-up initiatives like Odisha's Jaga Mission succeeded by addressing daily use, social context, and democratic participation.
True urban aspiration requires professional expertise, evidence-based inquiry, and situated knowledge rather than top-down political fantasy detached from ground realities.
sum.text:
Dream projects are common in Indian politics. Almost every politician has a dream project that often becomes an extension of their persona. The Smart Cities Mission was the biggest dream project in Indian history, and now that the Mission has ended, its record invites closer scrutiny. Can politicians just dream up urban development projects? A critical inquiry into the SCM reveals that political dreaming cannot be allowed to masquerade as urban planning.
Dream projects tend to begin with advertisements of radical transformation that prove their feasibility through state narratives, rather than expert input or citizen experience — often even before the first brick is laid. The SCM was no different.
The SCM was sold as a future-facing vision of urban India through narratives of integrated command centres, digitisation, and selected pockets of redevelopment. It promised to deliver urban development across the diverse landscape of India under the vague quality of smartness. This vagueness made SCM powerful as a political narrative. It allowed governments to package very different interventions under a single glamorous label and circulate them as proof of modern governance. It was an effective national public-relations machine.
Like all other dream projects, the image of promised transformation was sustained through the device of the showcase. The Mission’s Area-Based Development model concentrated resources in bounded precincts where rapid visual change could be staged and photographed as transformation. For example, a 2025 study by Sarbeswar Praharaj found that, across the 100 cities, SCM interventions reached less than 10 per cent of the population, and in 41 cities, the ABD area covered less than 10 per cent of municipal territory and just 5 per cent of total population. In cities such as Ludhiana, Ahmedabad, and Jaipur, areas affecting only 0.5 per cent of the city received around 20 per cent of total investment. In other words, the mission produced enclaves of display and then promoted those enclaves as the city.
Dream projects, therefore, privilege what can be seen over what is needed, what can be inaugurated over what is sustainable, and what can be advertised over what citizens experience. While a command-and-control centre, a “smart” road, or a digitally branded service platform travels well in photographs and speeches, cities are made habitable through good drainage, affordable housing, and ward-level repair. Sadly, they do not make good visual…

sum.text: GST Council is scheduled to meet next week after a one-year hiatus. One assumes the reform process initiated through GST 2.0 at its last meeting in September 2025 should be taken further. Rate compression and rationalisation — by which the number of GST rates were reduced to 5% and 18% slabs, and for almost all items of common consumption dropped to 5% — rejuvenated aggregate economic demand. This has been endorsed in two separate KPMG and Deloitte surveys earlier this year. GoI’s assessment that the growth in demand would more than compensate for immediate fall in revenues seems to have played out. After an initial slump in growth rates of monthly GST collections in Q3 FY26 (except for May 2026), growth rates have been above 7.5%, touching 15.8% in July. Net revenue collections (cumulative Centre and states) from GST grew at 9.2% during April-July 2026 compared to the same period of FY26. Most respondents in the two surveys stressed the need for further structural and procedural reform. An important one is the review of input tax credit (ITC) scheme, in order to remove legal, procedural and administrative bottlenecks in its flow across the value chain. In an ideal VAT system, taxes paid on supplies at the previous stage of the value chain are allowed to be set off against liability at each successive stage, so that the burden of tax falls only on the end consumer, and not businesses constituting the chain that are only pass-through entities. If there are blockages in this flow, stranded credit becomes a cost to business, resulting in ‘cascading’. The current GST system has several blockages, some enshrined in law (e.g., restrictions on type of input goods or services for which credit is available); others structural (e.g., non-availability of ITC on some petro products since they fall outside GST’s purview; rate inversions between input services and output goods), or operational (e.g., non-transferability of ITC from one state to another within the same business entity). The combined impact of these on the cost structure of businesses is significant. Absorbing these costs for some time may be possible. But, if sustained, businesses will be compelled to pass them on to end-consumers by increasing prices. Also, such blockages place domestically-supplied goods and services at a disadvantage vis-à-vis imports that enter the country after full neutralisation of embedded indirect taxes in their country of origin. points: India has strengthened wildlife laws and anti-poaching enforcement, but timely adjudication of forest and wildlife cases remains a critical missing link.
Thousands of forest and wildlife cases remain pending in courts for years, causing witnesses to disperse, evidence to fade, and deterrence to weaken.
The core issue is a lack of systematic implementation rather than a lack of recommendations, as various committees have urged fast-track courts for decades.
As far back as 2006, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology recommended fast-track courts for settling wildlife crime cases.
Subsequent bodies like the 2010 Elephant Task Force and the National Wildlife Action Plan 2017-2031 also envisaged fast-track courts for wildlife offences.
Assam designated district judge cadre courts as fast-track courts following action by the Gauhati High Court to expedite Wildlife Protection Act cases.
In July 2022, the MoEFCC communicated recommendations for special judicial mechanisms to states and UTs following a frontline staff committee report.
In November 2025, during T N Godavarman proceedings concerning Corbett Tiger Reserve, the Supreme Court recorded expert committee calls for fast-track courts.
States can consult high courts to map pendency and designate existing courts or dedicated benches without building an expensive new court network.
sum.text:
India has spent decades strengthening wildlife laws, expanding protected areas, and improving anti-poaching enforcement. Yet one critical link has received comparatively less attention: timely adjudication. Thousands of forest and wildlife cases remain pending before courts across the country. When cases remain unresolved for years, witnesses become difficult to trace, officials are transferred, evidence becomes harder to present, and deterrence can weaken. India does not suffer from a lack of recommendations on this issue. It suffers from a lack of systematic implementation.
As far back as 2006, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment, and Forests observed that fast-track courts for quick settlement of wildlife crime cases could contribute significantly to conserving endangered species such as tigers, elephants, and rhinos. The Union environment ministry noted the recommendation for necessary action.
The Elephant Task Force, in its 2010 report Gajah: Securing the Future for Elephants in India, recommended fast-track special courts for wildlife offences. The National Wildlife Action Plan 2017-2031 also envisaged fast-track courts for wildlife cases.
Following action by the Gauhati High Court, courts in Assam were designated to expedite the disposal of cases under the Wildlife (Protection) Act and other forest laws. Its 2016-17 annual report recorded designation of courts in the district judge cadre as fast-track courts.
A committee constituted by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) to examine working conditions of forest frontline staff recommended special judicial mechanisms for environment and forest-related cases. In July 2022, the Ministry communicated the recommendations to states and Union Territories, seeking timely action.
Fast-track special courts for rape and POCSO cases were launched in 2019; hundreds are functioning and have disposed of lakhs of cases. Separately, 879 general fast-track courts were functioning across 22 states and UTs as of December 31, 2025.
The comparison is institutional, not between the nature or gravity of these offences. India has demonstrated that where categories of cases require specialised and timely adjudication, dedicated judicial capacity can be created. But merely calling a court “fast-track” cannot guarantee speedy justice.
That lesson applies directly to wildlife crime. The problem is not pendency alone. The National Wildlife Action Plan itself…

Diffuse surveillance involves watch shared among states, private companies and foreign vendors, creating a system where no single actor is answerable.
State interest in identifying people predates Aadhaar by over 150 years, starting with British magistrate William Herschel taking handprints in 1858.
While the state-centred right to privacy was established in the 2017 Puttaswamy judgment, current data protection frameworks struggle to check diffuse actors.

sum.text:
Rajya Sabha member A.A. Rahim has petitioned the SC against the Delhi Police’s use of facial recognition and biometric surveillance during the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) protests.
The SC has upheld the Election Commission’s (EC) Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, which critics warned could exclude eligible voters.
What it is: Diffuse surveillance is watching shared among states, private companies and foreign vendors , not one identifiable actor. It is like cameras run by many owners, with nobody answerable for the whole.
An old impulse: State interest in identifying people predates Aadhaar by over 150 years . In 1858 , British magistrate William Herschel took handprints on contracts, later developed into Bengal’s fingerprint classification system .
What is new: The scale and speed differ, visible in Aadhaar, Delhi’s cameras and the SIR.
The takeaway: A privacy law that checks one actor at a time cannot protect data passing through many hands.
Facial recognition by the state: Rahim’s petition alleges police used facial recognition, AI-enabled smart glasses , drones and a mobile command vehicle at Jantar Mantar . Two private firms hosted the data.
Doxxing by online networks: Women at the CJP protests later had their personal details published, with reported rape and death threats .
Public shaming precedent: In March 2020 , Uttar Pradesh put photos and addresses of Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 protesters on Lucknow hoardings. The Allahabad High Court ordered removal as an “unwarranted interference in privacy” .
Identity checks on the rolls: Under the SIR, identity checks decide who stays on the electoral roll. The SC held the EC may examine citizenship only for this purpose, not decide it.
Scale of the SIR: Bihar’s roll fell from about 7.89 crore to 7.42 crore electors.
Meaning: Doxxing is publishing a person’s private details, such as a home address, online so that others can find and target them.
Speed of exposure: A photo can be uploaded, identified, amplified and linked to an address within hours .
Remedy so far: Disposing of the PIL, the SC left remedial measures to Union Ministries.
State-centred right: A nine-judge Bench in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) held privacy a constitutionally protected right. The case was against the state, so its test targets state action .

The Supreme Court failed to provide strong procedural and substantive safeguards against the misuse of power, instead legitimising the entire exercise without proper checks.

sum.text:
Rarely in the annals of Indian constitutional history have two key institutions, the Supreme Court of India and the Election Commission, acted in tandem with such shameless disregard for the constitutional purpose of their office, inflicting administrative cruelty on citizens and disenfranchising them . The SIR enterprise, which in principle may be justified, was so badly conceived and executed that it has left citizens reeling. But worse still, at almost every opportunity to set things right, these institutions have responded mendaciously, failing to address any of the core concerns their critics have raised about the fairness and ease of the SIR process. Ritika Chopra and Damini Nath’s reporting in this paper highlighted important questions about the functioning of the Commission. But they were not merely procedural questions. They raised serious substantive questions. The opaque process, including the software protocols, was shifting the burden of proof onto citizens. These days, nothing is shocking. But still, the idea that the Election Commission files appeals en masse against 16 lakh voters in West Bengal who had been found eligible for inclusion is stunning indeed.
The SIR mess is the joint effect of the Supreme Court and ECI. The Election Commission has the power to ensure the integrity of voting lists. The independence of the Commission requires that the removal of the Commissioners be by impeachment. The only practical mechanism of accountability was therefore the Supreme Court. It should have, without infringing on the Commission’s powers, insisted on the strongest possible procedural and substantive safeguards against the misuse of that power. But the net effect of Court intervention was to legitimise the whole exercise, without any real safeguards. Worse still, the Court, via Justice Joymalya Bagchi, gave ad hominem remarks suggesting those who were excluded could simply vote in the next election. They sent a powerful signal that voting rights can be treated casually. Green hydrogen produced without carbon emissions could be a substitute for fossil fuels in most of the ‘hard to abate’ sectors.
We have now fortunately reached an inflection point where we can leapfrog and become an advanced green industrial economy as early as in the next decade. India has a decisive cost advantage as the price of solar power and storage in the country is one of the lowest in the world. The price is now lower than new thermal power when our domestic coal is the cheapest fossil fuel in the world.
With this cost advantage of carbon free electricity, the input cost of converting the water molecule into green hydrogen through electrolysis, is now amongst the lowest in the world. This has been clearly seen in the recent SECI bid for the supply of green ammonia, whose primary production cost is green hydrogen, in which the contract price of ₹53.3 per kg, is comparable to the price of imported urea, far lower than expected. This also demonstrated that inviting bids for a long-term supply contract for a new product is the best way to get low prices.
It is bringing in private investment for the first time for the manufacture of green ammonia. Inviting bids for long term supply would bring in private investment for green hydrogen and all downstream carbon free products using green hydrogen. This is an effective policy instrument where there is no demand in the market.

points: A recent court ruling held that OpenAI's storage of ANI's work for training large language models is protected as fair dealing under Section 52(1)(a) of the Copyright Act.
The court reasoned that training a model is a form of research for generating new knowledge, despite the legislature not anticipating AI when amending the Act in 2012.
The finding that OpenAI's use is private has been criticized because the data is ultimately put to a commercial purpose rather than a non-paying, non-commercial one.
To determine fairness, the court assessed if usage was limited to training, caused economic competition, and if ChatGPT served the overall public interest by aiding scientific research.
Critics argue that if content producers lose revenue to keep producing material, LLMs will eventually lack quality data to train on, questioning the limits of fair use.
Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 exempts intermediaries from liability, but whether this applies to LLMs that generate content rather than host it remains legally unsettled.
The government stated in the Lok Sabha in July that intermediary liability depends on the service's functions, showing ongoing uncertainty nearly four years after AI products arrived.
India's broader AI legal architecture remains thin, relying on voluntary commitments in AI Governance Guidelines rather than statutory mandates.
A major legal gap is the absence of a liability regime for AI systems, as traditional laws require an intention or state of mind that AI models lack.
sum.text:
The first claim is of greater salience. On that, the court held that OpenAI’s storage of ANI’s work for training purposes was protected by Section 52(1)(a) of the Copyright Act, which provides that a “fair dealing” with any work for the purposes, among other things, of “private or personal use, including research” shall not constitute an infringement of copyright.
That the use might constitute research of some kind may not be especially debatable. The court reasoned that research is ordinarily a closed, intermediary activity, and that training a model could well be seen as “a form of research for generating new knowledge.” The court was candid about the difficulties it faced. When Section 52 was last amended in 2012, the legislature, Justice Amit Bansal wrote, could not have imagined the advent of AI.
The court’s finding that OpenAI’s research was for private use is rather more controversial. The judge relied on the Supreme Court’s judgment in Academy of General Education, Manipal v. B. Malini Mallya (2009), where it found that a ballet performed at an educational institution constituted private use. “Open AI stores the literary works in a closed space without access to the public,” wrote Justice Bansal. “The said data is not publicly available to any human entity either for access or for download. Therefore, in my opinion, the use amounts to being purely private.”
This finding is harder to justify. Section 52(1)(a)(i) is only concerned with what a dealing was for. It does not require an examination of who can see the file afterwards. In this case, the actual deployment of data may well be secretive, but it scarcely follows that the use is therefore a private one. The judgment in Malini Mallya related to a dance before a non-paying audience at a college. There was no element of commerce at stake. Here, however, the data is put to an ultimately commercial purpose.
For something to constitute fair dealing, it must not only be restricted to the purposes itemised in the statute; the dealing must also be fair. To determine the fairness of the use, the court asked itself three questions: whether OpenAI’s use of the plaintiff’s copyrighted work was limited to training its LLMs; whether the usage resulted in any economic competition to the detriment of the plaintiff; and whether the functions performed by ChatGPT served the overall public interest.

The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) has recently extended the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act (AFSPA), 1958, for another six months from 1 October 2026 in specified areas of Manipur, Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh , following a review of the security situation.
AFSPA is a central law that gives special powers to the armed forces in areas officially declared as “ disturbed ” to help them tackle insurgency and serious internal security threats.
The primary objective of AFSPA is to provide the armed forces (including the Army, Air Force, and paramilitary forces) with special legal immunity and powers necessary to control internal conflict, militancy, and insurgency in regions where the civil administration and police are deemed incapable of maintaining law and order.
AFSPA was first promulgated in 1942 , by Linlithgow , in response to the Quit India Movement in 1942. Its aim was “to confer special powers upon certain officers of the armed forces.
After Independence, the Act was retained by the ordinance enacted in 1958 , to control increasing violence in the North-eastern States, which the State governments found difficult to control.
In simple terms, AFSPA gives armed forces the power to maintain public order in “disturbed areas”.

sum.text:
The Union Ministry of Home Affairs has extended Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act (AFSPA), 1958 for another six months from October 1, 2026, in parts of Manipur, Nagaland and Arunachal Pradesh. In Manipur, the entire State remains a “disturbed area”, except the jurisdictions of 13 police stations in five Valley districts. The extension comes amid the continuing security concerns following the ethnic conflict that began on May 3, 2023, which reversed the earlier reduction of AFSPA-covered areas in the State.
Purpose of the Act: AFSPA gives armed forces special legal powers to maintain public order in areas where State authorities face serious insurgency and internal security problems.
Meaning of Disturbed Area: Under Section 3, an area can be declared disturbed because of differences or disputes between different religious, racial, language, regional, caste or community groups.
Authority to Declare: The Central and State Governments can declare an area disturbed. For Union Territories, the administrator can also make such a declaration.
Duration of Declaration: A disturbed-area declaration continues until it is revoked. The Supreme Court has stressed that such declarations should be time-limited and reviewed periodically.
Geographical Application: AFSPA, 1958 currently applies in parts of the Northeast. Jammu and Kashmir has a separate Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1990.
Use of Force: Armed forces may use force, including lethal force after due warning, against persons acting in contravention of prohibitory orders, subject to the Act.
Arrest Without Warrant: Personnel can arrest a person without a warrant when the conditions prescribed under AFSPA are met.
Search Without Warrant: Armed forces can enter and search premises without a warrant, enabling action during security operations.
Restriction on Gatherings: Armed forces can prohibit gatherings of five or more persons in a disturbed area.
Control of Firearms: The armed forces can ban the possession of firearms in areas where AFSPA is in force.
Protection from Prosecution: Prosecution or other legal proceedings for acts done or purportedly done under AFSPA require prior sanction from the Central Government.
Manipur Before 2023: AFSPA had operated in Manipur since 1981. Its application was withdrawn from the Imphal municipal area in 2004.

sum.text:
BENGALURU: Space regulator-cum-promoter IN-SPACe has issued new guidelines for hosted payloads, requiring authorisation for Indian payloads hosted on foreign satellites while exempting foreign payload owners from separate authorisation when their payloads are hosted on Indian satellites. The framework recognises a “Satellite as a Service” (SaaS) model, letting Indian entities offer satellite capacity to Indian or overseas customers by providing the bus and associated systems, with or without ITU filings, ground stations or payload operations support. Such satellites may be considered for National Registry of Space Objects.
The guidelines, dated Sept 17 under Indian Space Policy-2023, cover instruments, transponders and other systems owned by one entity but housed in another’s satellite bus, or on a launch vehicle’s orbital stage such as the PSLV Orbital Experimental Module (POEM). They classify payloads into three categories: Indian-owned payloads on non-Indian satellites; Indian or non-Indian payloads on Indian satellites; and payloads on POEM or similar platforms. Uses include remote sensing, communications, science, meteorology, navigation, technology demonstrations, in-orbit experiments and space situational awareness.
Indian entities placing payloads on Indian or foreign satellites need mandatory IN-SPACe authorisation, for single or multiple payloads including constellations. Authorisation ends with the host agreement or the host satellite’s operational life, whichever is earlier. For Indian payloads on foreign satellites, the owner retains absolute decision-making powers over operations, and the foreign host bears all liability risks and must indemnify the owner and GoI.Foreign payloads on Indian satellites are treated differently.
The owner need not separately seek IN-SPACe authorisation. Instead, the Indian host must disclose the payload while applying for authorisation of the host satellite and submit its agreement with the owner. The foreign owner must hold approvals from its own administration and indemnify the host and govt for third-party claims.
The host retains control of the satellite and must be able to switch off the hosted payload or cease its emissions if directed by IN-SPACe or govt for reasons including national security, radio-frequency interference or other critical concerns. Chief Secretary Anand Bardhan flagged off the team from the state secretariat on Tuesday.“This initiative will be a milestone in understanding the risks and reducing the threat of glacial lake outburst floods in the years ahead,” Bardhan said.
Advanced sensors, satellite communications and real-time data monitoring would help scientists track changes in the lake, he added. It is the first scientific team being sent to a glacial lake in Uttarakhand’s high Himalayas to establish a monitoring and early warning system. Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami said close monitoring of glacial lakes and associated risks was essential given Uttarakhand’s location in the high Himalayas.“The installation of an early warning system at Vasundhara Tal is an important step towards strengthening the state’s disaster preparedness through technology and a scientific approach,” Dhami said.
"The government would work with scientific institutions, experts and disaster management agencies to expand modern monitoring and warning capabilities across high-altitude areas," he added. The Uttarakhand State Disaster Management Authority (USDMA) is coordinating the expedition under the National GLOF Risk Mitigation Programme. The BJP Legislature Party had moved a motion seeking the Speaker’s removal, but Sharma claimed the motion was not accepted. Sharma accused the ruling National Conference and the Congress of trying to divert attention from governance failures by raising contentious political issues. He specifically challenged the Congress to clarify its position on Articles 370 and 35A. Reaffirming the party’s stance, Sharma said the BJP would continue to support statehood for Jammu and Kashmir but firmly oppose any attempt to link it with demands for a return to the pre-1953 position or the restoration of Articles 370 and 35A. The party, he added, would take this opposition across the Union Territory.

explain.headline: Formation, Classification, Weather Sequence, and Occlusion of Mid-Latitude Frontal Systems
static: An air mass is a large body of air with relatively uniform temperature and moisture characteristics acquired from its source region.
Frontogenesis is the process of creation or intensification of a front, typically occurring in sub-polar low-pressure belts where contrasting air masses converge.
A cold front forms when a cold air mass actively wedges under and displaces a warm air mass, causing rapid uplift and heavy precipitation.
A warm front develops when a warm air mass slides gently over a retreating wedge of colder air, producing steady, widespread precipitation.
An occluded front forms when a cold front overtakes a warm front, creating a complex weather pattern and marking the mature stage of a mid-latitude cyclone.

points: Fronts are dynamic transition zones formed when two contrasting air masses meet, serving as the framework for mid-latitude weather systems.
Frontogenesis is the basic mechanism of front formation, driven by the convergence of warm and cold air masses with different temperatures and densities.
Fronts are classified into principal types according to their relative air-mass movement, including cold, warm, stationary, and occluded fronts.
The weather sequence during a frontal passage shows how atmospheric conditions progressively change before, during, and after the system moves through.
A mid-latitude frontal system brings predictable shifts in temperature, pressure, wind direction, and cloud cover as it transitions.
Occlusion occurs when a faster-moving cold front catches up with a warm front, lifting the warm sector completely off the ground.
The process of occlusion modifies the warm sector and gradually transforms a mature cyclone towards its declining and dissipating stage.
Understanding frontal dynamics explains the life cycle of extra-tropical cyclones and the continuous redistribution of heat and moisture globally.

Beneficence requires the state to act in ways that benefit citizens, particularly vulnerable populations needing welfare and social protection.
Autonomy represents the capacity of an individual to make an informed, uncoerced decision regarding their own life and choices.
Ethical governance seeks a balance where welfare measures do not erode the fundamental moral agency and constitutional rights of citizens.
explain.what: Administrative paternalism is a governance approach where the state implements welfare-oriented interventions, creating an ethical tension between protecting citizens from harm and respecting their personal autonomy.
explain.why_in_news: The concept features in ethics evaluation frameworks to test civil-services aspirants on the balance between state welfare duties and citizen dignity.
explain.background: Administrative paternalism explores how welfare policies can sometimes overlap with coercive state control over individual decision-making.
significance: Crucial topic for Ethics (GS Paper IV) regarding governance, integrity, and public service values.
Helps bureaucrats navigate the fine line between public welfare delivery and protecting individual liberty.
Addresses the ethical dimensions of policymaking concerning vulnerable populations.
explain.mains: What do you understand by administrative paternalism? Under what circumstances can paternalistic decision-making undermine the autonomy and dignity of citizens?

points: Administrative paternalism refers to welfare-oriented state interventions where authorities make decisions on behalf of citizens to protect them from harm.
The core ethical dilemma involves balancing the state's duty of care or beneficence with the citizen's right to autonomy and self-determination.
Paternalistic decision-making becomes problematic when excessive interventions become coercive, infantilising, or exclusionary towards citizens.
Such interventions undermine personal dignity and moral agency by completely disregarding informed choices and active citizen participation.
The structural approach to administrative paternalism requires evaluating when protective measures cross the line into controlling behavior.
Best practices in public administration suggest favoring minimum necessary interference alongside maximum possible citizen agency.
Empowerment and supported decision-making should always take precedence over unnecessary bureaucratic control and top-down restrictions.

Key Demand of the question Explain the meaning and ethical basis of administrative paternalism, including the tension between beneficence and autonomy . Identify the circumstances in which paternalistic intervention ceases to be protective and begins to undermine choice, dignity and agency . Structure of the Answer: Introduction Introduce paternalism through the ethical tension between protecting citizens from harm and respecting their capacity for self-determination . Body Meaning and ethical basis: Explain administrative paternalism as welfare-oriented intervention and briefly indicate the underlying beneficence–autonomy dilemma with an administrative illustration. Threat to autonomy and dignity: Show how excessive or unjustified paternalism can become coercive, infantilising or exclusionary , especially when informed choice and citizen participation are disregarded. Conclusion Conclude with the principle of minimum necessary interference and maximum possible agency , favouring empowerment and supported decision-making over unnecessary control.

sum.text:
The Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved the ‘Green Energy Corridor Phase-III’ scheme with an outlay of Rs 1.86 lakh crore to set up an intra-state transmission system with battery storage to evacuate 135 GW of renewable energy. This is significant in view of India’s ambitious target of 500 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2030. According to an official statement, the Union Cabinet chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi approved the Green Energy Corridor Phase-III (GEC-III) scheme.
This initiative will strengthen India’s Intra-State Transmission System (InSTS) to enable evacuation of up to 135 gigawatt (GW) of renewable energy across states/ Union territories. The scheme also provides for deployment of 50 GWh of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) at the Renewable Energy (RE) developer/generator end or any other location of importance for grid flexibility to address intermittency, congestion, peak-hour curtailment and meet non-solar hour demand. The scheme will facilitate grid integration and power evacuation within the states/UTs of India.
The scheme is targeted to be set up by FY 2032-33 with total project outlay of Rs 1,86,405 crore, comprising Rs 1,36,378 crore for the development of Intra-State Transmission Systems (InSTS) under GEC-III, Rs 50,000 crore for 50 GWh of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS). The scheme involves a total central financial support of Rs 54,082 crore. The central financial assistance will help in offsetting the intra-state transmission charges and thus keep the power costs down.
Thus, the government support will ultimately benefit the end users – the citizens of India. All Greenfield projects under the InSTS component will be implemented through the Tariff Based Competitive Bidding (TBCB) mode, while brownfield upgradation and network strengthening works will be executed under Cost Plus Basis (CPB). The state transmission utilities will be the overall implementing agency, and Transmission Service Providers (TSPs) will participate under TBCB on a Build-Own-Operate-Maintain (BOOM) model.
The scheme will help in achieving the target of 900 GW installed non-fossil capacity by 2035. The scheme will also contribute to long-term energy security of the country and promote ecologically sustainable growth by reducing carbon footprint. It will generate large direct and indirect employment in the power sector, manufacturing, and construction industries.

explain.headline: Cabinet Approves Minimum Support Prices for Rabi Crops for Marketing Season 2027-28
static: Minimum Support Price (MSP) is a form of market intervention by the Government of India to insure agricultural producers against any sharp fall in farm prices.
The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) takes the final decision on fixing MSPs based on recommendations of the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP).
CACP recommends MSPs after evaluating production costs, inter-crop price parity, supply-demand dynamics, domestic and global market prices, and agricultural terms of trade.
The government announces MSPs for 22 mandated crops plus sugarcane, which is covered under Fair and Remunerative Prices (FRP).
The mandated crops include 14 kharif crops, 6 rabi crops, and 2 commercial crops.
Union Budget 2018-19 announced that MSP would be fixed at least 1.5 times the all-India weighted average cost of production.

explain.background: The government fixes MSPs for mandated agricultural crops based on CACP recommendations to provide remunerative returns to farmers over their cost of production.
significance: Provides financial certainty and remunerative returns to farmers across 324 metric tonnes of procurement with an estimated payout of Rs 90,962 crore.
Maintains a margin of at least 50 percent over the cost of production, fulfilling the Union Budget 2018-19 mandate.
Serves as the vital benchmark for government crop procurement and influences cropping choices and market pricing.

points: The Union Cabinet approved the Minimum Support Price policy for six Rabi crops for the Rabi Marketing Season 2027-28.
The decision aims to ensure remunerative prices to growers for their produce and covers 324 metric tonnes of procurement.
The policy involves an estimated payout of Rs 90,962 crore to farmers across the country.
The absolute highest increase in MSP was announced for Safflower at Rs 675 per quintal, followed by Rapeseed and Mustard at Rs 413 per quintal.
Increases for other crops include Rs 390 for lentil, Rs 136 for barley, Rs 83 for gram, and Rs 25 for wheat per quintal.
Revised MSP for wheat is set at Rs 2,610 per quintal and barley at Rs 2,286 per quintal.
Pulse and oilseed support prices include gram at Rs 5,958, lentil at Rs 7,390, rapeseed and mustard at Rs 6,613, and safflower at Rs 7,215 per quintal.
The revised prices guarantee a margin of at least 50% over the projected all-India weighted average cost of production.
sum.text:
The Union Cabinet has approved the Minimum Support Price policy for six Rabi crops for the Rabi Marketing Season 2027-28, involving an estimated payout of ₹90,962 crore to farmers across 324 metric tonnes of procurement. Under the revised pricing, the MSP for wheat has been set at ₹2,610 per quintal, while barley stands at ₹2,286 per quintal. Among pulses and oilseeds, gram has been fixed at ₹5,958 per quintal, and lentil at ₹7,390 per quintal.
The support price for rapeseed and mustard has been pegged at ₹6,613 per quintal, while safflower will fetch ₹7,215 per quintal. points: The Ministry of Power has notified the new Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE-3) norms for passenger vehicles, effective from April 2027 to March 2032.
The new rules remove a separate concession proposed earlier for small petrol cars weighing up to 909 kg following opposition from leading automakers.
The core issue involves balancing fleet-wide carbon dioxide emission targets while promoting cleaner technologies through a revised weight-adjustment formula and credit mechanism.
The reference vehicle weight has been increased from 1,082 kg under existing norms to 1,229 kg under the final rules, providing more relief to lighter vehicles.
The fuel-consumption benchmark is tightened from 3.996 litres per 100 km in 2027-28 to 3.3273 litres per 100 km in 2031-32, marking a 16.7 percent improvement.
The framework includes a super-credit system where one battery electric or range-extended electric vehicle is counted as three vehicles.
Strong hybrids running on flex-fuel get a 2.5x factor, strong hybrids get 1.6x, and flex-fuel vehicles get a 1.1x factor.
A credit-debit system is introduced, allowing manufacturers performing better than emissions targets to earn credits and others to accumulate debits.
sum.text:
New Delhi, Sep 30 The government has notified new corporate average fuel economy (CAFE-3) norms for automakers, removing a separate concession proposed for small petrol cars. The norms that were notified by the Ministry of Power will come into effect from April 2027 and remain in force until March 2032. However, the Centre had proposed a 3 grams per km concession for petrol cars weighing up to 909 kg in the previous year.
The concession was opposed by several leading automakers. Moreover, the final rules do not provide a separate concession for cars below 909 kg. Instead, the government has changed the formula used to calculate a manufacturer's fleet-wide carbon dioxide emissions target.
The reference vehicle weight has been increased to 1,229 kg from 1,170 kg in the September 2025 draft. The final rules also use a lower annual weight adjustment. The changes provide relatively more relief to lighter vehicle fleets while making the targets stricter for heavier fleets.
Under the final formula, a 909-kg car has an FY28 emissions target of about 82.8 grams of CO2 per km, compared with about 76 grams under the September 2025 draft. But for a 2,500-kg vehicle, the target is about 142.4 grams under the final formula, compared with about 151.4 grams under the earlier formula. In addition, the final CAFE-3 rules also retain incentives for cleaner vehicles through a super-credit mechanism.
One battery electric vehicle will be counted as three vehicles for calculating a manufacturer's fleet performance. The same 3x factor applies to range-extended electric vehicles. Plug-in hybrids and strong hybrids running on flex-fuel will get a 2.5x factor, while strong hybrids will get a 1.6x factor.
Flex-fuel vehicles will get a 1.1x factor. Additionally, the rules also introduce a credit-debit system. Manufacturers that perform better than their emissions targets will earn credits, while those falling short will accumulate debits.

sum.text:
The Centre has approved procurement worth 5,547.99 crore rupees at Minimum Support Price (MSP) under the Price Support Scheme (PSS) for major pulses and oilseeds in Uttar Pradesh, Karnataka and Telangana for the Kharif Marketing Season 2026-27. The Agriculture Ministry has said that the decision has been taken to protect farmers from a fall in market prices and ensure remunerative returns for their produce.
Talking about the decision, Union Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said the Centre is working with full commitment towards the welfare of farmers, increasing their incomes and making the agriculture sector self-reliant. Mr Chouhan noted that the government is firmly committed to ensuring that farmers get a fair price for their produce, and the procurement system is being made more transparent and accessible. Under the approval, large-scale procurement of various crops will be undertaken from farmers in the three states. Uttar Pradesh has been allocated the largest share, with procurement worth 3,992.57 crore rupees. This includes 4.66 lakh metric tonnes of tur worth 3,937.70 crore rupees and 6,250 metric tonnes of moong worth 54.87 crore rupees. In Karnataka, procurement worth 1,107 crore rupees has been approved. The state will see procurement of 1,15,500 metric tonnes of soybean valued at 659.27 crore rupees, 38,250 metric tonnes of moong valued at 335.83 crore rupees, and 13,413 metric tonnes of sunflower valued at 111.90 crore rupees. For Telangana, the Centre has approved procurement worth 448.42 crore rupees. This includes 62,000 metric tonnes of soybean valued at 353.90 crore rupees and 10,766 metric tonnes of moong valued at 94.52 crore rupees.
Mr. Chouhan said the measure will provide economic security to farmers and encourage production of pulses and oilseeds, contributing to India’s self-reliance in pulses and edible oils. He added that procurement arrangements at all designated centres will remain transparent and farmers will receive payment for their produce directly into their bank accounts in a time-bound manner.

sum.text:
The Union Cabinet on Tuesday approved the extension of the Jal Jeevan Mission till December 2028 with a significantly enhanced financial outlay and a restructured implementation strategy focused on long-term service delivery in rural drinking water supply.
The Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, approved a proposal of the Ministry of Jal Shakti to transform the programme from a primarily infrastructure-driven initiative to a citizen-centric utility model ensuring sustainable piped potable water supply in rural areas.
Under the revised framework, the total outlay for the mission has been increased to Rs 8.69 lakh crore, with central assistance of Rs 3.59 lakh crore, up from Rs 2.08 lakh crore approved during the mission’s launch in 2019–20. The increase represents an additional central share of Rs 1.51 lakh crore.
As part of structural reforms, the government will introduce a national digital framework called “Sujalam Bharat”, which will assign each village a unique Sujal Gaon or Service Area ID. The system will digitally map the entire drinking water supply chain—from source to household tap—to improve monitoring, transparency and accountability.
The programme will also strengthen community participation through initiatives such as “Jal Arpan”, under which Gram Panchayats and Village Water and Sanitation Committees (VWSCs) will formally participate in the commissioning and handover of water supply schemes. A Gram Panchayat will be able to declare itself “Har Ghar Jal” only after certifying that adequate operation and maintenance arrangements are in place.
To encourage community ownership of water systems, the mission will introduce “Jal Utsav”, an annual community-led event focused on reviewing and maintaining local water supply infrastructure while promoting collective responsibility for water sustainability.
When the mission was launched in 2019, only 3.23 crore rural households (17%) had tap water connections. Since then, more than 12.56 crore additional rural households have been connected.
According to government data, 15.80 crore out of 19.36 crore rural households, or about 81.6%, currently have tap water connections.
Studies by several institutions have highlighted the programme’s broader social impact. According to SBI Research, the mission has freed around nine crore women from the daily burden of fetching water. The petition said there was reasonable apprehension of bias against one of the judges who decided the case. The petition was filed by Congress leader Jaya Thakur, one of the petitioners challenging the CEC & ECs (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.
On September 23, a bench of justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma gave a split verdict on whether the petitions should be heard by a five-judge Constitution bench. They later passed a common order placing the matter before the Chief Justice of India (CJI) to constitute a five-judge bench. Thakur’s plea seeks recall of the September 23 order based on a “reasonable likelihood of bias,” as news reports indicated that the son of one of the judges (Justice Sharma) appears for the Election Commission of India (ECI) before the Madhya Pradesh High Court.
A curative petition is the last judicial recourse available to a litigant to overturn a verdict of the Supreme Court. Two days after the judgment was delivered, reports surfaced that justice Sharma’s son represents the ECI among other government panels before the Madhya Pradesh high court. Thakur stated that this fact was unknown to them during the hearing on the challenge to the 2023 law.

Adopted by consensus during the WTO’s 12th Ministerial Conference in Geneva in June 2022, the Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies is the first multilateral WTO agreement with an environmental sustainability objective. It entered into force on September 15, 2025, after securing acceptance from two-thirds of WTO members.
The Agreement targets subsidies related to marine wild capture fishing and fishing-related activities at sea, while explicitly excluding aquaculture and inland fisheries from its scope. This means India’s aquaculture sector, including its shrimp exports, remains unaffected by the new rules.
According to the Commerce & Industry Ministry, the Agreement aims to curb subsidies that contribute to illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing, as well as fishing of overexploited stocks, thereby promoting the conservation and sustainable use of marine resources.
The Ministry said the Agreement would help protect the livelihoods of traditional and small-scale fishers by discouraging unsustainable fishing practices while creating a more balanced global fisheries regime. It also disciplines harmful subsidies that support large industrial fishing fleets operated by distant-water fishing nations, a move expected to benefit countries such as India, where the fisheries sector is dominated by small-scale operators.
The Ministry said India’s accession to the Agreement would further strengthen its reputation as a responsible seafood exporter, improving access to premium international markets that increasingly prioritise sustainability and traceability. sum.text:
The Election Commission of India (ECI) has extended the timeline for the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Andhra Pradesh and Meghalaya, days after revising the schedule for Delhi and Maharashtra.
The decision was taken at a meeting of the full Election Commission on Wednesday, September 30, according to a press note issued by the poll panel. Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and Election Commissioners SS Sandhu and Vivek Joshi attended the meeting.
Under the revised schedule, the notice phase and disposal of claims and objections in Andhra Pradesh will continue until October 10, 2026. The final publication of the electoral roll in the state has been scheduled for October 16.
For Meghalaya, the final publication of the electoral roll has been fixed for October 26, 2026, according to the Election Commission's latest press note.
The latest extensions come shortly after the ECI revised SIR timelines in Delhi and Maharashtra, giving electors additional time to file claims and objections and allowing election officials more time to dispose of notices and objections.
In Delhi, the deadline for filing claims and objections was extended to October 30, while the disposal period was extended to November 30. The final electoral roll is now scheduled for publication on December 4, according to the revised timeline reported earlier.
In Maharashtra, the Commission extended the claims and objections period to October 12, with the disposal of notices and claims extended to November 10. The move followed a request from the state's Chief Electoral Officer.
The SIR exercise is aimed at revising electoral rolls, with the Election Commission stating that its objective is to ensure that no eligible citizen is left out while no ineligible person is included. The exercise involves verification of electoral-roll details and provides voters an opportunity to raise claims and objections.
The Commission had launched the latest phase of SIR across 16 states and three Union Territories in May. The exercise covers a large electorate and involves Booth Level Officers (BLOs) undertaking field-level verification.
The latest decision means electoral authorities in Andhra Pradesh and Meghalaya will get additional time to complete the remaining stages of the revision process. For voters, the extended timelines provide more time to respond to notices, raise objections or seek corrections where required.

The additions highlight India's rich cultural heritage, ancient rock-cut architecture, and medieval temple styles spanning different dynasties and historical periods.
The core issue involves preserving and globally recognizing India's diverse historical monuments through official UNESCO listings.
The Bagh Caves in western Madhya Pradesh comprise nine rock-cut Buddhist viharas carved along the Baghani River during the Satavahana period.
Out of the nine original Bagh caves, five survive, featuring notable murals on walls and ceilings painted using the tempera technique.
Cave 4 of the Bagh complex is known as Rang Mahal, while Cave 2 is popularly called the Pandava Cave and is the best-preserved monastery.
The Group of Temples of the Chambal Valley in Morena district, Madhya Pradesh, showcases the regional Nagara style built between the 8th and 11th centuries CE.
These Chambal valley temples include the Bateshwar temple, Padavali Temple Complex, Kakarmath temple, and the circular Chausath Yogini Temple at Mitaoli.
These sites demonstrate advanced ancient and medieval structural engineering techniques, such as dry masonry using interlocked sandstone blocks without mortar.

The Bagh caves are located on the southern slope of the Vindhyan range in western Madhya Pradesh.
They are situated on the banks of the Baghani River.
These are not natural but were carved over a period of time during the Satavahana period.
Features: They consist of nine rock-cut Buddhist caves . The were excavated on a perpendicular sandstone rock face of a hill across the seasonal stream of Baghani. These rock-cut Buddhist monasteries are renowned for their stunning mural paintings, which illustrate the Jataka tales. The earthy reds, yellows, and greens of the murals offer a rare glimpse into the spiritual and artistic traditions of ancient Buddhism. Out of the original nine caves, only five have survived, all of which are viharas or resting places for monks, having a quadrangular plan . Cave 4 , also known as the Rang Mahal, is the most important of the five caves that still exist (Palace of Colors). Tempera was used to paint the Viharas of Bagh’s walls and ceilings , with shards still evident in Caves 3 and 4 (remnants also observed in Caves 2, 5, and 7). Cave 2 is popularly known as “Pandava Cave” and stands as the best-preserved rock-cut monastery in the complex .

Employment in the registered manufacturing sector continued to expand, an official release said.
Total emoluments paid to the workforce also increased by 12.08 per cent in 2024-25 as compared to 2023-24. Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh and Haryana were the five leading states in terms of the number of persons engaged in the manufacturing sector in 2024-25. Two out of twelve villages inside the reserve were relocated to reduce human interference and improve forest health.

sum.text:
A three-year-old tigress was flown in from Bihar’s Valmiki Tiger Reserve to West Bengal’s Buxa Tiger Reserve on Wednesday, nearly eight years after the National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) reported no tigers in Buxa, as the state prepares to reintroduce the big cat on October 2. This marks the first tiger reintroduction in the eastern state. Officials said plans were afoot and discussions were being held with other states to bring in at least six more tigers to introduce in BTR in the next two years.“The tigress reached the Hasimara air force base around 6:40 am on Wednesday, from where she was taken to the BTR by road in a special animal transport vehicle.
She will be released in the reserve’s core zone on October 2,” a senior official of the state forest department said. The “Status of Tigers in India – 2018” published by the NTCA said that no tigers were recorded in three reserves in India, including Buxa, Dampa and Palamau.“The report, however, also offered a ray of hope as it stated that tigers could be repopulated in BTR after restoration of the prey base. The planning started back then, and the tiger reintroduction is the culmination of eight years of effort,” another official said.
The official said that while tiger reserves like Corbett, Nagarhole and Bandipur registered very high chital densities of 71 per sq km, 24 per sq km and 51 per sq km respectively, the chital density in Buxa had dwindled to just around 5 per sq km. Officials said that over the years, around 870 chital deer from various zoos and parks across the state were released in the BTR to increase the reserve’s prey base. Of the 12 villages, two were relocated.“It was an uphill task.
To maintain a healthy tiger population means the entire forest health needs to be healthy, starting from the forest, the prey base, water availability and least human interference,” a forest official said. A former forest official said, “For tigers we needed more grasslands and not very dense forest cover which are mostly wooded forests. For this the canopy needs to be opened up so that sunlight can reach the ground and grasses can grow.
This would in turn help bring back the herbivores and tigers would follow them.” In December 2021, a tiger was spotted in the BTR after a gap of more than two decades. sum.text:
The Union Cabinet -- chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi -- on Wednesday approved the India-Saudi Arabia Bilateral Investment Protection Agreement (BIPA), a treaty aimed at protecting and facilitating investments by Indian and Saudi investors in each other’s countries.
The development is seen as providing greater legal certainty to investors while strengthening investment ties between the two countries.
With substantial mutual investments between India and Saudi Arabia, the agreement seeks to protect the interests of investors from either country in the territory of the other while facilitating further expansion of bilateral investments. The deal includes investor-friendly provisions covering aspects such as treatment of investments, non-discriminatory treatment, expropriation and free transfers. These provisions are expected to provide greater certainty to investors and support confidence in cross-border investments.
Saudi is India’s fourth largest trade partner, while India is Saudi Arabia’s second largest trade partner. Bilateral trade between the two countries reached $41.88 billion in 2024-25, with chemicals and petrochemicals contributing 10 per cent, which is nearly $4.5 billion.
The BIPA is set to provide a framework for protecting investments made by investors from India and Saudi Arabia in each other's territories.
The pact is aimed at creating greater legal certainty around investments and facilitating increased investment engagement between the two countries.
Such provisions are intended to ensure that investors receive a defined level of protection while making investments in the other country.
The BIPA includes provisions on expropriation, providing protection to investors in relation to the taking of investments.
This is among the provisions aimed at providing greater confidence to investors while making cross-border investments.
It provides for free transfers, another provision aimed at facilitating investment flows between India and Saudi Arabia.
The inclusion of investor-friendly provisions is expected to support greater confidence among investors and encourage further bilateral investment.
The two-year requirement provides investors enhanced access to the Investor State Dispute Settlement (ISDS) mechanism.
ISDS provides a window to investors to seek settlement of investment-related disputes with the state, subject to the terms and conditions set out in the agreement.
